solution.concept_anchor: CBDT statutory basis — Central Board of Revenue Act 1963
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because CBDT administers the Income Tax Act, 1961 so extensively that most students conflate administration of an Act with establishment under it.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): CBDT administers the Income Tax Act, 1961 but was NOT established under it.
Eliminate (c): The Constitution does not establish CBDT; it is a statutory, not a constitutional, body.
Eliminate (d): The Finance Act contains annual tax amendments but is not the parent statute of CBDT.
Confirm (b): CBDT derives its statutory existence from the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap here is the conflation between the statute a body administers and the statute under which it is created. CBDT administers the Income Tax Act, 1961 so prominently that candidates assume it was established under that very Act. The Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963 — a far less examined piece of legislation — is the actual parent statute. A partially prepared student will confidently pick (a) and lose the mark.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT is a statutory body — meaning it derives its existence from a specific Act of Parliament, not from the Constitution or from executive order alone. The enabling legislation is the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963, which bifurcated the original Central Board of Revenue into CBDT (direct taxes) and what later became CBIC (indirect taxes).
• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Income Tax Act, 1961 is administered by CBDT, not the legislation under which CBDT was established.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963 is the founding statute.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: CBDT is a statutory body, not a constitutional body; it finds no mention in the Constitution.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Finance Acts amend tax law annually but do not create administrative bodies.
Value Addition:
• CBDT and CBIC share the same parent statute — Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963.
• Being a statutory body, CBDT's powers and structure can be modified by Parliament.
• CBDT falls under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.

solution.concept_anchor: CBIC renaming from CBEC in 2018

statement_analysis.statement: Both CBDT and CBIC are statutory bodies established under the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963.
statement_analysis.reason: The Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963 is the common parent statute that created both bodies by bifurcating the earlier unified Central Board of Revenue.

statement_analysis.statement: CBIC was formerly designated as the Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC) and was renamed in 2019 to reflect its expanded GST mandate.
statement_analysis.reason: CBEC was renamed CBIC in 2018, not 2019; the renaming followed the GST rollout in July 2017 and the consequent need to reflect its expanded mandate over goods and services tax.

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT exercises administrative control over the Income Tax Department while CBIC administers customs and GST field formations.
statement_analysis.reason: This correctly captures the jurisdictional boundary: CBDT handles direct taxes (income tax), while CBIC handles indirect taxes including GST, customs, and residual central excise.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because the year difference between 2018 and 2019 is a one-year gap that many candidates overlook, and the substance of the renaming context (GST) is correctly stated in Statement 2, making it feel wholly accurate.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Both CBDT and CBIC trace their statutory origin to the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963 — Statement 1 is correct.
Verify Statement 2: CBEC was renamed CBIC in 2018, not 2019 — Statement 2 is incorrect; eliminate options that treat it as correct.
Verify Statement 3: The jurisdictional split described is accurate — Statement 3 is correct.
Only option (c) captures '1 and 3 only' — confirm (c) as correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 embeds a one-year temporal trap. The renaming of CBEC to CBIC occurred in 2018, but candidates who remember the GST context (2017 launch) may not fix the exact renaming year and accept '2019' as close enough. UPSC frequently exploits single-year gaps to test precision of recall rather than mere awareness of an event.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT and CBIC are twin statutory bodies created by bifurcating the earlier Central Board of Revenue, both governed by the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963. Their parallel structure under the same ministry with different tax mandates is a recurring UPSC comparison point.
• Statement 1 — Correct: The shared legislative parentage of CBDT and CBIC under the 1963 Act is unambiguous.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CBEC was renamed CBIC in 2018 — one year after the GST launch in July 2017. The 2019 date is a deliberate temporal trap.
• Statement 3 — Correct: CBDT controls the Income Tax Department; CBIC controls customs, GST, and central excise field formations — the jurisdictional split is accurate.
Value Addition:
• Both CBDT and CBIC report to the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance.
• CBIC's renaming to reflect 'Indirect Taxes and Customs' was necessitated by GST subsuming several indirect taxes.
• Separate cadre control means IRS (Income Tax) officers serve CBDT; IRS (Custom and Indirect Taxes) officers serve CBIC.

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT composition — IRS cadre, executive appointment

statement_analysis.statement: The CBDT is a single-headed body led by a Chairman who exercises all powers independently without a collegium of members.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT is headed by a Chairman supported by multiple members (typically six), making it a multi-member body, not a single-headed one.

statement_analysis.statement: Positions on CBDT are open to lateral entry from the private sector, reflecting the government's broader push for domain expertise.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT members are senior officers from the IRS (Income Tax cadre); lateral entry has not traditionally been a feature of CBDT composition.

statement_analysis.statement: Because CBDT adjudicates tax disputes between the state and taxpayers, it is classified as a quasi-judicial body under Indian administrative law.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT is primarily an administrative and policy-making body; adjudication of disputes happens before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and courts, not before CBDT itself.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because many candidates conflate CBDT's powerful role with a strong single-headed structure, and the phrase 'independently without a collegium' sounds like an administrative arrangement that could plausibly exist.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: CBDT has a Chairman AND typically six members — it is not single-headed; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: CBDT membership is drawn exclusively from senior IRS (IT cadre) officers; no lateral entry provision exists — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: CBDT does not adjudicate disputes; it is an administrative body — Statement 3 is incorrect.
All three statements are incorrect; the option listing all three as 'NOT correct' is (d) — confirm (d).
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's composition and character are frequently misunderstood because of its significant authority over tax policy and administration. Clarity on three key points resolves all three statements.
• Statement 1 — Incorrect: CBDT has a Chairman plus typically six members; it is a collegiate body, not a single-headed authority.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: All CBDT members belong to the IRS (Income Tax cadre); the body has not been opened to lateral entry from the private sector.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: CBDT is an administrative and policy body. Tax disputes are adjudicated by the Commissioner (Appeals), ITAT, High Courts, and the Supreme Court — not by CBDT.
Value Addition:
• CBDT members are appointed by the President of India on the Finance Ministry's recommendation.
• Being an administrative body, CBDT's decisions are subject to judicial review.
• The distinction between administrative bodies (CBDT) and quasi-judicial bodies (ITAT) is a recurring UPSC theme.

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT Circulars vs Notifications — legal force hierarchy

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT Circulars bind Income Tax officers in their administrative functioning.
statement_analysis.reason: Circulars issued by CBDT are binding on Income Tax Department officers, directing how they exercise discretionary powers.

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT Circulars have statutory force equivalent to provisions of the Income Tax Act and thus override conflicting sections of the Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Supreme Court settled in the UCO Bank case that CBDT Circulars cannot override statutory provisions; they operate within the framework of the Act.

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT Notifications issued under specific sections of the Income Tax Act carry statutory force and are binding on all parties including courts.
statement_analysis.reason: Notifications are issued under the delegated legislative authority of specific Income Tax Act sections and possess statutory force, unlike Circulars.

statement_analysis.statement: A taxpayer may rely on a beneficial CBDT Circular even though Circulars are technically not binding on taxpayers — a principle recognized by judicial interpretation.
statement_analysis.reason: Indian courts have held that where a CBDT Circular is beneficial to the taxpayer, the taxpayer may claim its benefit even though the circular binds officers, not the taxpayer directly.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is a strong distractor because a candidate who correctly identifies Statement 2 as wrong but is uncertain about Statement 4 (judicial interpretation angle) may hesitate and stop at three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is clearly correct — Circulars bind Income Tax officers, a settled principle.
Statement 2 is incorrect — the UCO Bank Supreme Court ruling explicitly held that Circulars cannot override the Income Tax Act's statutory provisions.
Statement 3 is correct — Notifications derive statutory force from their enabling sections in the Income Tax Act.

Statement 4 is correct — courts have permitted taxpayers to claim benefit of favorable Circulars despite Circulars not technically binding taxpayers; three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct — answer is (b) Only two... wait: statements 1, 3, and 4 are correct = three correct statements = option (c). Re-check: Only one incorrect = three correct out of four = 'Only three' = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the planted trap: CBDT Circulars are highly authoritative internal instruments, and a student who knows they bind officers may extend that logic to conclude they also override the statute — a classic scope-extension error. The UCO Bank case is the judicial anchor that limits Circulars strictly to operating within the Act, not above it.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT issues three categories of instruments — Circulars, Notifications, and Instructions — each carrying different legal weight, a distinction tested directly by UPSC.
• Statement 1 — Correct: Circulars bind Income Tax officers and direct their exercise of discretionary powers.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Supreme Court in UCO Bank case held unequivocally that Circulars cannot override statutory provisions of the Income Tax Act. Circulars operate within, not above, the statute.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Notifications issued under specific sections of the IT Act are subordinate legislation with genuine statutory force, binding on all including courts.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Indian judicial precedent allows taxpayers to claim the benefit of a favorable Circular even though Circulars formally bind officers, not taxpayers.
Three statements (1, 3, 4) are correct.
Value Addition:
• Instructions are the weakest category — internal administrative directions with no external legal force.
• This three-tier hierarchy (Notifications > Circulars > Instructions) is a direct tax practitioner's foundation.
• The UCO Bank ruling is essential case law for CBDT instrument classification questions.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because swapping Vivad se Vishwas with Sabka Vishwas as an indirect-tax scheme feels intuitive to a student who knows one but not both schemes, and the DTAA placement in List II item 3 sounds plausible for CBIC given customs has treaty elements.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap pairs Vivad se Vishwas and Sabka Vishwas — two similarly named dispute resolution schemes administered by different boards. A partially prepared student remembers 'Vishwas scheme = tax disputes' but does not distinguish which scheme belongs to CBDT (direct taxes) and which to CBIC (indirect taxes). This entity-swap is a classic UPSC trap in the matching format.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests four distinct CBDT-related concepts simultaneously — dispute resolution, international taxation, judicial precedent on Circulars, and comparative awareness of CBDT/CBIC schemes.
• A — 4: Vivad se Vishwas Scheme 2020 was administered exclusively by CBDT for direct tax disputes; its indirect-tax counterpart was Sabka Vishwas (CBIC).

• D — 3: The UCO Bank case is the Supreme Court ruling that definitively held CBDT Circulars cannot override statutory provisions of the Income Tax Act.
Value Addition:
• Vivad se Vishwas II was launched in 2024, extending the scheme's reach.
• APAs (Advance Pricing Agreements) are administered under CBDT's transfer pricing framework, not under DTAA provisions directly.
• CBDT shares tax information internationally under FATCA and CRS frameworks as India's designated competent authority.

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT Circulars binding on officers not taxpayers — policy body character
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because some candidates know that Circulars do not bind taxpayers and incorrectly infer that Reason R is therefore false, missing that R is a separate accurate statement about CBDT's administrative (not quasi-judicial) character.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? CBDT Circulars bind Income Tax officers but are not binding on courts or taxpayers — Yes, A is correct.
Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? CBDT is primarily an administrative and policy body, not a quasi-judicial authority — Yes, R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? CBDT Circulars bind officers rather than taxpayers because CBDT is an administrative body issuing internal directions, not a legislative or judicial body issuing universally binding norms — Yes, R explains A.
Both A and R are correct and R explains A — correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap operates here for candidates who think the relationship runs the other way: some students know Circulars do not bind taxpayers and assume this makes R (CBDT as administrative body) incorrect, whereas in fact R is the causal explanation for why Circulars bind only officers — internal administrative directions flow downward to subordinate officers, not outward to citizens. Recognising this causal direction requires understanding institutional character, not just isolated facts.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT occupies a unique position as an apex administrative body that issues policy instruments of varying legal force. The assertion-reason pair here tests whether students understand why Circulars have the binding scope they do.
Assertion (A): Correct — CBDT Circulars bind Income Tax Department officers in the exercise of their functions but do not bind courts or taxpayers. The Supreme Court in the UCO Bank case confirmed this distinction.
Reason (R): Correct — CBDT is an administrative and policy-formulation body, not a quasi-judicial or legislative body. It cannot create law binding on citizens; it directs its own subordinate officers.
Causal relationship: R correctly explains A. Because CBDT is an administrative body issuing internal instructions to its own field formations, the binding effect logically extends to those formations alone — not to external parties like taxpayers or courts. A quasi-judicial or legislative body would produce instruments with broader external effect.
Value Addition:
• Notifications issued by CBDT under specific IT Act sections do have statutory force — distinguishing them from Circulars is essential.
• CBDT Instructions are even lower in the hierarchy — purely internal with no claimed external force.
• The UCO Bank Supreme Court ruling remains the settled judicial authority on the binding scope of CBDT Circulars.

solution.concept_anchor: GAAR implementation year — Assessment Year 2018-19
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because candidates who remember 'GAAR was delayed multiple times' often anchor on the 2012 Shome Committee discussions and place GAAR's actual start in that era, missing that implementation finally happened from AY 2018-19.
elimination_logic: GAAR was originally proposed and debated prominently in the 2012-13 budget context following the Vodafone tax case — this is the earliest event.
The Shome Committee recommended a two-year deferral of GAAR — this happened in 2012-13, before formal rules were framed.
GAAR rules were formally notified and the framework was finalised in 2015-16 for prospective implementation.
GAAR became operationally applicable from Assessment Year 2018-19 — this is the latest event; correct order is Event 3 → Event 1 → Event 4 → Event 2, which maps to option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: GAAR's tortured implementation history makes chronology questions particularly trap-rich. The concept was announced, deferred, re-examined by committees, re-notified, and finally operationalized — each stage separated by years. Candidates who remember 'GAAR was delayed' but not the specific sequence will likely place the Shome Committee recommendation after the formal rules notification, which is reversed. The AY 2018-19 operative date is the sharpest precision point.
solution.final_explanation:
GAAR's journey from proposal to implementation stretched nearly a decade and is a rich source of chronology traps.
Correct sequence:
1. Vodafone judgment and GAAR debate in Union Budget 2012-13 — GAAR first gained national prominence following the retrospective tax controversy.
2. Shome Committee recommendations (2012) — the Expert Committee led by Parthasarathi Shome recommended a two-year deferral and significant safeguards.
3. Formal GAAR Rules notification and prospective applicability confirmed — the government finalised rules in 2015-16 with a deferred start.
4. GAAR made operative from Assessment Year 2018-19 — after multiple delays, CBDT began applying GAAR from AY 2018-19 onwards.
Why wrong options fail:
• (a) and (c) place Shome Committee after rules notification — historically reversed.
• (d) places AY 2018-19 implementation before the Shome Committee — impossible.
Value Addition:
• The GAAR invocation threshold is tax benefit exceeding ₹3 crore per year.
• An independent Approving Panel provides a safeguard against arbitrary GAAR invocation by tax officers.
• GAAR does not apply to Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) who are residents of DTAA countries.

solution.concept_anchor: Faceless Assessment exceptions — search and international tax matters
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because 'Faceless Assessment applies to all income tax assessments without exception' is the common understanding promoted in government communications about the scheme, and the existence of specific carve-outs is not widely known.
elimination_logic: Identify the scenario: a search-and-seizure operation has been conducted; the resulting assessment is a search assessment under Section 153A/153C.
Recall that Faceless Assessment under Section 144B explicitly excludes certain categories — search assessments are among the excluded categories.
Eliminate (a): Faceless Assessment does not apply universally to all cases; search assessments are carved out.
Eliminate (b) and (d): The scenario involves a search assessment carve-out, not a question of CBIC jurisdiction or GAAR applicability; confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap operates when students generalise 'Faceless Assessment = all income tax assessments' without knowing the statutory exceptions. Section 144B carves out search assessments, international taxation matters, and certain other categories. A candidate with surface knowledge of the Faceless Assessment Scheme will apply it to the scenario without checking the exception list — a very common UPSC trap design for flagship government schemes.
solution.final_explanation:
The Faceless Assessment Scheme, introduced under Section 144B of the Income Tax Act, is a landmark administrative reform aimed at eliminating physical interaction between taxpayers and assessing officers. However, the scheme does not apply universally to every assessment.
In the given scenario, the assessment arises from a search-and-seizure operation — this constitutes a 'search assessment' governed by Section 153A/153C, which is explicitly excluded from the Faceless Assessment framework.
• Option (a) — Incorrect: Faceless Assessment does not cover all income tax cases; search assessments are a statutory exclusion.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: CBIC has no jurisdiction over income tax assessments; this is purely a CBDT domain matter.
• Option (c) — Correct: Because the assessment arises from a search operation, it falls under the exclusion to the Faceless Assessment Scheme and will proceed through the conventional channel.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: GAAR is an anti-avoidance provision unrelated to the procedural question of faceless vs. conventional assessment.
Value Addition:
• International taxation matters and cases transferred for special audit are also excluded from Faceless Assessment.
• The Faceless Appeals Scheme similarly has exclusion categories.
• Faceless Penalty Scheme was introduced as the third pillar of the faceless ecosystem.

solution.concept_anchor: PAN statutory basis — Section 139A of Income Tax Act
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Section 139AA is closely associated with PAN-Aadhaar linkage, which is so prominent in CBDT communications that candidates may misidentify it as the primary PAN-issuing provision rather than the Aadhaar-linking provision, causing them to doubt (b) as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify what links three items: PAN, Aadhaar-PAN linkage, and CBDT's administration of PAN all fall under Income Tax Act provisions.
Section 139A governs issuance of PAN — correctly under CBDT/IT Act.
Section 139AA mandates Aadhaar-PAN linking — correctly under IT Act.
Binoy Viswam case upheld Aadhaar-PAN mandatory linkage — correctly related to PAN/Aadhaar.
Equalisation Levy is collected by CBDT but is NOT part of the Income Tax Act — it is governed by Finance Act provisions separately; this is the odd one out — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Equalisation Levy trap is a high-value UPSC knowledge point: CBDT collects the levy, so students associate it with the Income Tax Act, but it was introduced as a separate chapter in the Finance Act (2016) and was never incorporated into the Income Tax Act. This conflation between the collecting authority and the governing statute is a precision trap that separates prepared candidates from those with only surface awareness.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of the four items relate directly to PAN administration and its linkage with Aadhaar under provisions of the Income Tax Act; the fourth item relates to a different tax instrument entirely.
• Option (a): Section 139A — the enabling provision under the IT Act for issuing PAN; directly part of PAN administration.
• Option (b): Section 139AA — the mandatory Aadhaar-PAN linking provision under the IT Act, upheld in Binoy Viswam (2017).
• Option (c): Binoy Viswam case — Supreme Court judgment directly validating the Aadhaar-PAN linkage requirement; part of the PAN-Aadhaar legal story.
• Option (d): Equalisation Levy — collected by CBDT but governed by Finance Act provisions, NOT by the Income Tax Act. It is a charge on digital transactions by foreign companies and stands apart from the PAN/Aadhaar cluster.
Value Addition:
• Equalisation Levy was introduced in 2016 (6% on digital advertising) and expanded in 2020 (2% on e-commerce operators).
• In 2024, the government announced withdrawal of the 2020 Equalisation Levy expansion.
• PAN inoperativity consequences include higher TDS deduction rates — a CBDT enforcement tool.

solution.concept_anchor: DTAA overrides domestic law only if beneficial — Section 90(2)

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 90(2) of the Income Tax Act, a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) overrides the provisions of domestic tax law only when its provisions are more beneficial to the taxpayer.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 90(2) explicitly provides that whichever is more beneficial — the DTAA or the domestic law — shall apply to the taxpayer, making DTAA supremacy conditional on taxpayer benefit, not automatic.

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT's role in Advance Pricing Agreements (APAs) is limited to unilateral APAs within India; bilateral and multilateral APAs involving foreign tax authorities are exclusively handled by the Ministry of External Affairs.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT serves as India's competent authority for all APAs including bilateral and multilateral APAs; the Ministry of External Affairs has no role in transfer pricing negotiations, which are conducted through the Mutual Agreement Procedure (MAP) under CBDT's authority.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both statements contain accurate-sounding details — Section 90(2) is correctly cited and the APA description sounds plausible to a student who knows MEA handles international negotiations generally.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 90(2) provides the 'more beneficial' rule — DTAA overrides domestic law only when favorable to the taxpayer; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: CBDT is India's competent authority for bilateral and multilateral APAs; MEA has no role in transfer pricing APAs — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a plausible-sounding conflation between international negotiations generally (MEA's domain) and technical transfer pricing competent authority negotiations (CBDT's domain). A student who knows 'MEA handles India's international engagements' may incorrectly assign bilateral APA negotiations to MEA without knowing that CBDT's competent authority function is a specialised technical role separate from diplomatic functions.
solution.final_explanation:
International taxation is a growing UPSC focus area under CBDT's mandate. Two distinct principles are tested here.
• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 90(2) of the Income Tax Act embodies the 'beneficial rule' — between the DTAA and domestic law, whichever is more beneficial to the taxpayer prevails. DTAA does NOT automatically override domestic law in all situations.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CBDT is India's designated competent authority for all APAs — unilateral, bilateral, and multilateral. Bilateral APAs involve negotiations with foreign tax authorities conducted by CBDT through the MAP mechanism, not through MEA. Assigning this function to MEA is a classic entity-conflation error.
Value Addition:
• India's APA programme is among the most active globally since its launch in 2012.
• Transfer pricing regulations under Sections 92–92F empower CBDT to prescribe methods for determining arm's length prices.
• The General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR) interact with DTAAs — GAAR can override treaty benefits in cases of tax avoidance arrangements.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because many candidates associate the Right to Information Act with citizen rights against government bodies and may reason that taxpayer rights would flow from the same instrument rather than from a dedicated provision in the IT Act.
elimination_logic: The Taxpayer Charter was introduced in 2020 as a statutory commitment by CBDT — it must have a statutory basis within tax law.

Section 144B governs Faceless Assessment — eliminates (c).

solution.concept_anchor: Equalisation Levy — not part of Income Tax Act, Finance Act governed
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because students who know CBDT collects the Equalisation Levy assume it must be governed by the Income Tax Act, making the pairing in (d) feel correct even though it misrepresents the governing statute.
elimination_logic: Evaluate (a): Section 115BAA introduced a reduced corporate tax rate of 22% for existing domestic companies under the 2019 Ordinance — this is correctly matched.
Evaluate (b): Section 115BAB applies to new manufacturing companies set up after October 2019 — the 15% rate is for new manufacturing companies, not all new companies; (b) is incorrectly matched.
Evaluate (c): Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) rate was not specifically reduced under the 2019 Ordinance for all companies; (c) conflates MAT with the standard rate reduction.
Evaluate (d): Equalisation Levy is governed by Finance Act provisions, NOT by the Income Tax Act — (d) is an incorrect match.
Only (a) is correctly matched — confirm (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (d) exploits the conflation between collection authority and governing statute. Because CBDT collects Equalisation Levy, students associate it with the Income Tax Act framework. However, Equalisation Levy was deliberately kept outside the Income Tax Act and is governed by separate Finance Act chapters. This structural distinction carries significant legal implications for treaty relief and is a precision UPSC point.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2019 corporate tax reforms via the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance were operationalized through specific sections inserted into the Income Tax Act by CBDT.
• Option (a) — Correct: Section 115BAA provides the reduced 22% tax rate for existing domestic companies that forgo certain exemptions and deductions — correctly matched.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Section 115BAB is specifically for new domestic manufacturing companies set up after 1 October 2019, offering a 15% rate — not all new companies.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: MAT provisions and rates were adjusted separately; conflating MAT reduction with Section 115BAA misrepresents the reform architecture.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Equalisation Levy is collected by CBDT but is governed by Finance Act provisions, not by the Income Tax Act — the governing statute distinction is the key trap.
Value Addition:
• Section 115BAB's 15% rate was a flagship incentive for manufacturing FDI (Make in India linkage).
• Companies opting for Section 115BAA or 115BAB are exempt from paying MAT.
• Equalisation Levy's exclusion from the IT Act means DTAA relief is not available against it.

solution.concept_anchor: Black Money Act 2015 — separate from IT Act; Benami law quasi-judicial character

statement_analysis.statement: The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015 is a standalone statute administered by CBDT and is distinct from the Income Tax Act, 1961.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2015 Act is an independent legislation targeting undisclosed foreign income and assets; it is not a provision within the Income Tax Act, though CBDT administers both.

statement_analysis.statement: The adjudication of Benami transactions is carried out by CBDT directly as part of its administrative enforcement function.
statement_analysis.reason: Benami transaction adjudication is a quasi-judicial function performed by an Adjudicating Authority constituted under the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 — CBDT does not directly adjudicate these cases.

statement_analysis.statement: The Income Declaration Scheme, 2016 was a one-time window administered by CBDT that allowed taxpayers to disclose previously undisclosed domestic income upon payment of tax, surcharge, and penalty.
statement_analysis.reason: The IDS 2016 was indeed a CBDT-administered amnesty scheme for domestic undisclosed income, distinct from the foreign asset disclosure scheme under the 2015 Black Money Act.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because all three statements contain accurate contextual elements (CBDT, Benami, enforcement) that make the entire set seem plausible, tempting candidates to select 'all three correct.'
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The Black Money Act 2015 is explicitly a standalone Act separate from the IT Act — Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: Benami adjudication is quasi-judicial, performed by an independent Adjudicating Authority, not by CBDT itself — Statement 2 is incorrect; eliminate options including Statement 2.
Statement 3: IDS 2016 was CBDT-administered for domestic undisclosed income — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct; option (c) captures '1 and 3 only' — confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is the partial-truth trap: CBDT does operate within the Benami enforcement ecosystem (through income tax search and investigation units that initiate Benami proceedings), creating the impression that CBDT directly adjudicates. However, the adjudicatory role is vested in a quasi-judicial Adjudicating Authority under the 2016 Act — CBDT's role is investigative and operational, not adjudicatory. The distinction between initiating action and adjudicating it is the precision UPSC tests.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's enforcement portfolio spans multiple special statutes beyond the Income Tax Act, creating a rich set of knowledge points on institutional boundaries.
• Statement 1 — Correct: The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015 is a self-contained statute distinct from the IT Act, targeting offshore undisclosed assets.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Benami transaction adjudication is the function of an Adjudicating Authority constituted under the 2016 Amendment Act. CBDT's units may investigate and refer cases but the adjudicatory function is quasi-judicial and independent of CBDT.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Income Declaration Scheme, 2016 was CBDT's amnesty window for domestic black money — different from the Black Money Act 2015 which targeted foreign assets.
Value Addition:
• Under the Benami law, confiscated benami property vests in the central government.
• The Black Money Act 2015 carries significantly harsher penalties (up to 90% tax+penalty) compared to IT Act provisions.
• IDS 2016 came in the context of demonetization and saw significant declarations before November 2016.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 138 IT Act — CBDT data sharing legal basis
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because CBDT's data-sharing with SEBI and RBI sounds like it would flow from a financial sector coordination framework or a FEMA provision, rather than from a specific section of the Income Tax Act, making (c) feel authoritative.
elimination_logic: Identify what governs CBDT's power to share taxpayer information with other regulators — this requires a specific statutory provision.
Eliminate (a): The Right to Information Act provides public access to information but does not govern inter-agency data sharing by CBDT.
Eliminate (c): No standalone 'Financial Intelligence Sharing Act' exists in Indian law — this is a plausible fabrication.
Eliminate (d): FEMA governs foreign exchange management; inter-agency domestic tax data sharing is not its domain.
Section 138 of the Income Tax Act specifically permits CBDT to share taxpayer information with other government bodies including CBIC, SEBI, and RBI — confirm (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (c) names a plausible-sounding legislation that does not exist. Students who know CBDT shares data with financial regulators but do not know the specific statutory basis will eliminate obvious wrong answers and be drawn to a fabricated but authoritative-sounding option. Section 138 of the IT Act is an obscure but testable provision — precisely the kind of precision UPSC rewards.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's ability to share taxpayer data with other regulatory bodies is not implied or general — it requires explicit statutory authorization to protect taxpayer confidentiality while enabling coordinated enforcement.
• Option (a) — Incorrect: The RTI Act enables public access to government information but does not authorize CBDT's inter-agency data transfers under a regulatory framework.
• Option (b) — Correct: Section 138 of the Income Tax Act specifically empowers CBDT to share information with other government agencies including CBIC, SEBI, and RBI — this is the legal basis for India's tax-financial intelligence coordination.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: No 'Financial Intelligence Sharing Act' exists in Indian law; this is a fabricated option.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: FEMA governs foreign exchange transactions; it does not authorize domestic tax data sharing between CBDT and financial regulators.
Value Addition:
• Project Insight is CBDT's data-mining initiative using third-party information to identify non-filers and under-reporters.
• Annual Information Statement (AIS) aggregates information from multiple sources including banks, mutual funds, and registrars.
• CBDT is India's competent authority under FATCA (with the USA) and CRS (global) for Automatic Exchange of Information.

solution.concept_anchor: TDS rate hierarchy — Finance Act vs CBDT notification

statement_analysis.statement: TDS rates specified in the annual Finance Act always override any different rates prescribed through CBDT notifications under the Income Tax Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The Finance Act and CBDT notifications under the Income Tax Act form a hierarchy where Finance Act rates are primary, but CBDT can modify rates within delegated authority — the statement's absolute 'always override' framing misrepresents the nuanced hierarchy where both sources interact within the statutory framework.

statement_analysis.statement: TRACES (TDS Reconciliation Analysis and Correction Enabling System) is a platform managed by CBDT that enables employers and deductors to file TDS returns, download certificates, and track TDS credits.
statement_analysis.reason: TRACES is correctly described as CBDT's digital TDS administration platform for reconciliation, return filing, and certificate generation.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 about TRACES is technically accurate and some candidates may misread the question (which asks for the NOT correct statement) and select (b) thinking they are identifying the correct one.
elimination_logic: Read the question carefully — it asks which statement is NOT correct.

Statement 1 uses 'always override' — an absolute qualifier; Finance Act rates are primary but CBDT notifications can prescribe rates under delegated authority; the absolute claim is incorrect — Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Statement 2 accurately describes TRACES — Statement 2 is correct (not the answer to a 'not correct' question).
The statement that is NOT correct is Statement 1 — option (a) identifies only Statement 1 as incorrect; confirm (a)... re-check options: (a) 1 only, (b) 2 only — so answer is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'always override' scope extension in Statement 1 is the trap. TDS rate-setting is a nuanced interaction between the Finance Act (primary legislation) and CBDT notifications (subordinate legislation under delegated authority). CBDT can and does prescribe rates through notifications in specific circumstances — so the absolute claim that Finance Act rates 'always override' is incorrect. A student who broadly knows Finance Act rates are 'more important' will accept Statement 1 without examining the absolute qualifier.
solution.final_explanation:
TDS administration sits at the intersection of legislative rate-setting and administrative operationalization, making it a nuanced area.
• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The relationship between Finance Act TDS rates and CBDT notification rates is hierarchical but not absolutely one-way. CBDT exercises delegated authority to prescribe or modify rates under specific Income Tax Act sections; the 'always override' claim overstates Finance Act primacy and ignores the delegated legislation framework.
• Statement 2 — Correct: TRACES is CBDT's technological backbone for TDS administration — deductors use it for return filing, deductees use it to verify TDS credits, and tax certificates (Form 16/16A) are generated through it.
Value Addition:
• Section 194P (senior citizens) exempts eligible seniors from filing ITRs if their bank deducts TDS on their behalf — introduced by Finance Act 2021.
• Lower or nil TDS certificates can be obtained from the Assessing Officer under Section 197.
• CBDT periodically issues notifications reducing TDS rates in response to economic conditions (e.g., COVID-19 rate reductions in 2020).

solution.concept_anchor: DTC drafts, Arbind Modi Committee, Section 115BAC as partial DTC

statement_analysis.statement: The Direct Tax Code was proposed as a comprehensive replacement for the Income Tax Act, 1961, with the primary objective of simplifying tax law and broadening the tax base.
statement_analysis.reason: The DTC's stated objective was to replace the complex Income Tax Act with simpler, modern legislation that would improve compliance and expand the tax base.

statement_analysis.statement: The Task Force on Direct Tax Code constituted in 2017 was chaired by Arbind Modi and submitted recommendations that were implemented in full through a new Direct Tax Code enacted by Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: The Arbind Modi Task Force submitted its report in 2019, but its recommendations were not implemented through a new DTC enacted by Parliament; instead, select recommendations were incorporated into the existing Income Tax Act incrementally.

statement_analysis.statement: The new tax regime under Section 115BAC of the Income Tax Act is considered a partial implementation of DTC principles, offering lower tax rates in exchange for forgoing most exemptions and deductions.
statement_analysis.reason: The simplified rate structure under Section 115BAC — lower slab rates with no exemptions — mirrors the DTC's core design philosophy and is widely described as partial DTC implementation.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the 2009 and 2013 DTC drafts were tabled before Parliament as Bills but were withdrawn due to disagreements between CBDT and the Finance Ministry on revenue implications.
statement_analysis.reason: The DTC drafts were released as discussion documents and a Bill was introduced but lapsed with the dissolution of Parliament; the characterization that withdrawal was due to CBDT-Finance Ministry disagreement is inaccurate — CBDT is advisory and does not have veto power in such decisions.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) 'Only two' is a strong distractor because Statement 3's characterization of Section 115BAC as 'partial DTC' is a nuanced claim that some candidates may doubt, potentially miscounting correct statements.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: DTC's replacement objective is accurately stated — correct.
Statement 2: Arbind Modi Committee recommendations were NOT fully enacted as a new DTC by Parliament — incorrect.
Statement 3: Section 115BAC's lower-rate-no-exemption design mirrors DTC philosophy — correct.
Statement 4: The DTC's failure is attributed to institutional disagreement which is inaccurate; the DTC Bills lapsed with Parliament dissolution — incorrect.
Two statements (1 and 3) are correct — answer is (b) Only two.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial truth: the Arbind Modi Task Force did exist and did submit a report, but attributing full parliamentary enactment to its recommendations is false — a classic partial-truth trap where the first half is accurate and the second half inserts a false outcome. Statement 4 similarly uses plausible-sounding institutional conflict to fabricate a reason for the DTC's non-implementation.
solution.final_explanation:
The DTC's long journey from proposal to non-implementation is a recurring policy reform question in UPSC prelims.
• Statement 1 — Correct: DTC was designed to replace the Income Tax Act, 1961 with simpler, consolidated legislation.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Arbind Modi Task Force (constituted 2017, reported 2019) made recommendations, but no new DTC was enacted; recommendations were incorporated piecemeal into the existing IT Act.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Section 115BAC's architecture (lower rates, no exemptions) reflects the core DTC philosophy and represents a partial implementation within the existing IT Act framework.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: DTC drafts lapsed with Parliament's dissolution; the characterisation of CBDT-Finance Ministry disagreement as the reason for withdrawal is factually unsupported.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — answer is Only two.
Value Addition:
• The DTC 2009 draft proposed a modified EET (Exempt-Exempt-Tax) system for savings instruments.
• Section 115BAC was made the default regime for individuals from AY 2024-25 onwards.
• The DTC's proposed Wealth Tax abolition was actually implemented — Wealth Tax was abolished in 2015.

solution.concept_anchor: Income Tax search — executive power, no prior judicial approval needed
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and the causal relationship (executive power → no prior judicial approval) sounds logically sound, leading many students to select (a) without verifying whether R is the precise legal explanation or merely a parallel true fact.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Search authorizations under Section 132 of the IT Act do not require prior judicial approval — this is a settled legal position; A is correct.
Step 2 — Is R correct? Unlike CBI/ED which operate under different procedural laws, income tax search powers are indeed executive in nature — R is correct as a factual statement.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? The absence of prior judicial approval in IT searches is not because of a contrast with CBI/ED; it is because Section 132 confers the authorization power directly on specified income tax authorities (Principal Directors). The comparison with CBI/ED, while factually true, is not the causal explanation for why IT searches don't need judicial pre-authorization — that flows from the specific statutory grant in Section 132 itself.
A correct + R correct + R does NOT explain A (R is a parallel fact, not the cause) — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a true-but-non-explanatory Reason. R correctly states that IT search powers differ from CBI/ED procedurally, which is a true fact. However, the reason IT searches don't require prior judicial approval is the specific statutory grant in Section 132 of the IT Act — not the contrast with CBI/ED. Making an accurate comparative statement the 'reason' for a separate legal feature is the classic option (b) trap in assertion-reason questions.
solution.final_explanation:
Income Tax search and seizure powers represent one of the most significant coercive tools in the CBDT arsenal, making their procedural character an important UPSC point.
Assertion (A): Correct — Under Section 132 of the Income Tax Act, the authorization for search and seizure is granted by specified Income Tax authorities (Principal Directors/Commissioners). No prior judicial approval (warrant from a court) is required before conducting the search — this is a pure executive power.
Reason (R): Correct as a factual statement — Income Tax search authorization is indeed an executive power, and CBI searches (under CrPC provisions) and ED searches (under PMLA/FEMA) have their own distinct procedural frameworks.
Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. The fact that IT searches don't need prior judicial approval is explained by Section 132's statutory grant of authority to executive officers — not by comparing this to CBI or ED procedures. R is a true parallel observation, not the cause of A.
Value Addition:
• Section 133A governs survey operations — lesser intrusion, no power to seize books of accounts.
• Post-search assessments must be completed within specific timelines under Section 153A/153C.
• Faceless Assessment does NOT apply to post-search assessments — an important exception.

solution.concept_anchor: Religious trusts vs charitable trusts — Section 11 exemption distinction

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Finance Act, 2020, charitable institutions registered under Sections 12A/12AB and 80G of the Income Tax Act were required to apply for fresh registration — existing registrations did not continue automatically.
statement_analysis.reason: The Finance Act 2020 overhauled the charitable trust registration regime, requiring all existing trusts to re-register under the new framework of Section 12AB; perpetual registrations were replaced with time-limited, renewable registrations.

statement_analysis.statement: Purely religious trusts that do not carry out any charitable activities are entitled to the same exemption from income tax as charitable institutions under Section 11 of the Income Tax Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 11 exemptions are available for charitable purposes; purely religious bodies without a charitable element do not qualify for Section 11 exemption — the distinction between religious and charitable-cum-religious institutions matters significantly.

statement_analysis.statement: Anonymous donations received by charitable institutions are taxed under Section 115BBC of the Income Tax Act, representing an anti-abuse provision administered by CBDT.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 115BBC taxes anonymous donations (donations where the identity of the donor is not revealed) received by specified charitable and religious institutions at a flat rate of 30%, serving as an anti-money laundering tool.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because candidates who know religious trusts receive partial exemption may read Statement 2's 'same exemption' as referring to the partial exemption and accept it as correct, not distinguishing between partial benefit and the complete Section 11 exemption denied to purely religious bodies.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Finance Act 2020 mandatorily required fresh registration for all charitable institutions — this is a known reform; Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2: Purely religious trusts without charitable activity do NOT qualify under Section 11 — the 'same exemption' claim is incorrect; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Section 115BBC taxing anonymous donations is an accurate anti-abuse provision — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (a) captures '1 and 3 only'; confirm (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a partial-truth trap: some religious trusts do receive tax benefits, leading students to assume the exemption framework treats religious and charitable trusts identically. The critical distinction is that Section 11's income exemption is available only where the purpose is 'charitable' (which includes religious if linked to public benefit) — purely religious purposes without charitable dimension are not covered. UPSC exploits this 'partially true, fully wrong' structure repeatedly in exemption questions.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's regulation of charitable and religious organisations underwent significant reform through the Finance Act 2020 and involves multiple anti-abuse provisions.
• Statement 1 — Correct: The Finance Act 2020 replaced the old perpetual registration system with time-bound registrations under Section 12AB, requiring all existing charitable institutions to re-register.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Section 11 exemption covers income from property held under a trust for charitable or religious purposes — but purely religious trusts without any charitable element do not automatically qualify. Charitable-cum-religious trusts get a partial exemption; purely religious bodies are excluded from Section 11.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Section 115BBC taxes anonymous donations at 30% — a key anti-abuse tool targeting donation-based money laundering through charitable institutions.
Value Addition:
• FCRA compliance is an additional layer — CBDT coordinates with MHA for foreign-funded NGO tax treatment.
• Section 80G deduction for donors was also brought under the Finance Act 2020 re-registration requirement.
• Section 12AB registration is now valid for 5 years and must be renewed, unlike earlier perpetual registrations.

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT delegated legislation — Income Tax Rules 1962

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT frames the Income Tax Rules, 1962 under its delegated legislative authority, which constitutes subordinate legislation supplementing the Income Tax Act, 1961.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT exercises rule-making power under the Income Tax Act and the Income Tax Rules, 1962 are a form of subordinate legislation — they fill in procedural and operational details that the parent Act empowers CBDT to prescribe.

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT's power to extend tax compliance deadlines through circulars is unlimited — it can effectively modify any statutory deadline prescribed under the Income Tax Act by issuing an administrative circular.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT's deadline extension powers are not unlimited — they operate within the framework of the Income Tax Act and judicial scrutiny; during the COVID-19 pandemic, many extensions were effected through executive orders and legislative backing where necessary, not purely through administrative circulars that override statute.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is unambiguously correct, and the pandemic-era deadline extensions were so visible and sweeping that many candidates assume CBDT has plenary power to modify any statutory deadline, making Statement 2 appear correct as well.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Income Tax Rules 1962 are indeed subordinate legislation framed by CBDT under delegated authority — Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: The claim of 'unlimited' deadline extension power is a scope-extension trap; CBDT's powers are bounded by statute and court oversight — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 'unlimited' qualifier in Statement 2 is the scope-extension trap. During COVID-19, CBDT issued numerous deadline extension notifications that appeared sweeping, creating the impression of plenary power. However, some extensions required legislative backing (through Taxation and Other Laws Ordinance 2020), confirming that CBDT cannot unilaterally override statutory deadlines through administrative circulars. The visible use of the power obscures its legal limits.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's rule-making and administrative powers sit within a structured hierarchy of statutory authority — extensive but bounded.
• Statement 1 — Correct: The Income Tax Rules, 1962 are CBDT's primary vehicle of subordinate legislation, covering forms, procedures, valuation methods, and other operational details the Income Tax Act empowers CBDT to prescribe.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CBDT does not possess unlimited power to extend statutory deadlines through circulars. Many pandemic-era extensions required the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Ordinance, 2020 — a legislative instrument — confirming that purely administrative circulars cannot override clear statutory deadlines.
Value Addition:
• CBDT's rule-making under the IT Act requires prior approval of the Central Government for rules to have statutory force.
• Rules framed by CBDT must be laid before Parliament under Section 295 of the IT Act.
• The hierarchy — Act > Rules > Notifications > Circulars > Instructions — determines the overriding effect in any conflict.

solution.concept_anchor: Vivad se Vishwas (CBDT) vs Sabka Vishwas (CBIC) — jurisdictional distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Vivad se Vishwas is widely associated with dispute resolution and students who know both schemes exist may swap their administering bodies, assigning Vivad se Vishwas to CBIC and Sabka Vishwas to CBDT.

solution.final_explanation:

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT classification — statutory not constitutional body

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT is a constitutional body because it derives authority from the Union List (List I) of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India, which vests taxes on income in the Union.
statement_analysis.reason: Being the subject of a Union List entry does not make a body 'constitutional' — constitutional bodies are those specifically created or mandated by the Constitution itself. CBDT is created by a parliamentary statute (Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963), making it a statutory body.

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT functions under the Department of Revenue within the Ministry of Finance and its administrative relationship with that department is distinct from being a constitutional body accountable to Parliament directly.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT operates as an administrative body under the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance — it reports through this executive channel, not as a constitutionally independent body reporting directly to Parliament.

statement_analysis.statement: The Finance Ministry exercises administrative control over CBDT, while CBDT retains functional autonomy in framing policy instructions and circulars for the Income Tax Department.
statement_analysis.reason: This captures the administrative vs. functional distinction accurately — the Finance Ministry has overall administrative authority, but CBDT exercises operational and policy authority over the Income Tax Department's field formations.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three correct' is a strong distractor because Statement 1 contains accurate facts (Union List, taxes on income) and students who conflate subject-matter constitutional coverage with institutional constitutional status will mark all three as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Union List Entry covering 'taxes on income' gives Parliament legislative authority — this does NOT make CBDT a constitutional body; CBDT is created by statute; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: CBDT's accountability flows through the Department of Revenue, not directly to Parliament as a constitutional body would — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3: The administrative-functional distinction between Finance Ministry and CBDT is accurately stated — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (b) captures '2 and 3 only'; confirm (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the conflation between constitutional subject-matter authority and institutional constitutional status. The Union List grants Parliament authority over income tax (Entry 82) — but CBDT's existence flows from a parliamentary Act, not from the Constitution itself. Constitutional bodies (like CAG, Election Commission, UPSC) derive their creation directly from constitutional provisions. CBDT has no such provision — a distinction that requires precise classification knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The classification of CBDT as statutory (not constitutional) is a foundational precision point that UPSC has tested through multiple angles.
• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The Union List's Entry 82 grants Parliament authority to legislate on income tax — but institutional classification (constitutional vs. statutory vs. executive) depends on whether the Constitution itself creates the body, not on whether the subject matter is in the Constitution. CBDT is statutory, created by the Central Board of Revenue Act, 1963.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CBDT's accountability flows through the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance — not independently to Parliament as constitutional bodies like CAG or the Election Commission operate.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The administrative-functional split is real — the Finance Ministry sets policy direction while CBDT exercises operational control over the Income Tax Department.
Value Addition:
• Constitutional bodies: CAG (Article 148), Election Commission (Article 324), UPSC (Article 315).
• Statutory bodies: CBDT, CBIC, SEBI, RBI — created by Acts of Parliament.
• Executive bodies: Created by government resolutions with no legislative backing — e.g., Planning Commission (now replaced by NITI Aayog).

solution.concept_anchor: GAAR invocation threshold — Rs 3 crore tax benefit
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Rs 1 crore is a psychologically round number that often appears in tax thresholds (TDS thresholds, high-value transaction reporting) and sounds authoritative in the GAAR context.
elimination_logic: Recall that GAAR has a minimum tax benefit threshold below which it cannot be invoked — this is a specific CBDT-prescribed figure.
Eliminate (a): Rs 50 lakh is below the actual GAAR threshold.
Eliminate (b): Rs 1 crore is a plausible but incorrect threshold.
Eliminate (d): Rs 5 crore would be too high; GAAR's threshold is Rs 3 crore.
The GAAR invocation threshold is tax benefit exceeding Rs 3 crore per year — confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: GAAR's tax benefit threshold of Rs 3 crore is an oddly specific number that sits between the common round numbers of Rs 1 crore and Rs 5 crore — making both (b) and (d) attractive to candidates who remember 'there is a crore-level threshold' but not the exact amount. UPSC exploits this precision gap, particularly for provisions with non-round quantitative thresholds.
solution.final_explanation:
GAAR cannot be invoked in every transaction with tax implications — it applies only when the tax benefit from an impugned arrangement exceeds a prescribed monetary threshold.
• Option (a) — Incorrect: Rs 50 lakh is below the GAAR threshold.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Rs 1 crore is a commonly cited figure in other tax contexts but is not the GAAR threshold.
• Option (c) — Correct: GAAR can be invoked only if the tax benefit involved exceeds Rs 3 crore in any assessment year — CBDT prescribes this as a procedural safeguard to prevent over-application.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Rs 5 crore sets the threshold too high; the actual figure is Rs 3 crore.
Value Addition:
• GAAR was made operative from Assessment Year 2018-19 after multiple deferrals.
• GAAR is applied after an independent Approving Panel reviews the case — a safeguard against arbitrary invocation.
• GAAR does not apply to arrangements where the main purpose is not tax avoidance even if tax benefits result.

solution.concept_anchor: Faceless Assessment three pillars and CPC Bengaluru

statement_analysis.statement: The Faceless Assessment Scheme comprises three pillars — Faceless Assessment, Faceless Appeal, and Faceless Penalty — all introduced as part of the same single notification in 2019.
statement_analysis.reason: While the three pillars are accurate (Assessment, Appeal, Penalty), they were introduced in phases, not through a single notification in 2019 — the Faceless Assessment was launched in 2019-20, with Faceless Appeals and Faceless Penalty following in subsequent phases.

statement_analysis.statement: The Centralized Processing Centre (CPC) at Bengaluru processes income tax returns without direct human interface and operates under CBDT's administrative framework.
statement_analysis.reason: CPC Bengaluru is CBDT's large-scale automated ITR processing centre that handles bulk return processing, refund generation, and mismatch identification without direct taxpayer-officer interaction.

statement_analysis.statement: Faceless Assessment under Section 144B of the Income Tax Act excludes search-based assessments and certain international taxation matters from its scope.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 144B explicitly carves out search assessments (under Section 132) and international taxation cases from the Faceless Assessment framework — these are handled through conventional channels.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) is a strong distractor because all three statements contain accurate core facts (the three pillars exist, CPC Bengaluru exists, the scheme is under Section 144B) and only a carefully trained eye spots the phased vs. single-notification error in Statement 1.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: The three pillars of faceless administration are correct but 'single notification in 2019' is wrong — they were rolled out in phases; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2: CPC Bengaluru processes ITRs without human interface under CBDT — Statement 2 is correct.
Statement 3: Section 144B excludes search assessments and international taxation matters — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are correct — option (a) captures '2 and 3 only'; confirm (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 embeds a temporal-scope trap: the three pillars are accurately named, but combining them into 'a single 2019 notification' is false. Candidates who know the three-pillar structure well will mark Statement 1 correct without questioning the implementation timeline detail. UPSC routinely injects false procedural or timeline details into otherwise accurate structural descriptions to test depth of preparation.
solution.final_explanation:
The Faceless Administration ecosystem is one of CBDT's most significant governance reforms and appears regularly in UPSC questions.
• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The three pillars (Assessment, Appeal, Penalty) are correctly identified, but they were rolled out in phases — Faceless Assessment began in 2019-20, with Faceless Appeals and Penalty Schemes introduced in 2020 and subsequently. A single 2019 notification covering all three did not exist.
• Statement 2 — Correct: CPC Bengaluru is a flagship CBDT infrastructure that processes crores of ITRs annually using automated systems, generating refunds and issuing intimations without direct human contact.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Section 144B's carve-outs for search assessments and international taxation cases are explicit — these categories involve complex, case-specific issues requiring conventional assessment channels.
Value Addition:
• Faceless Assessment eliminated the concept of a 'home jurisdiction' — cases are randomly assigned to assessing officers across India.
• The Taxpayer Charter 2020 (Section 119A) accompanied the Faceless ecosystem launch.
• Faceless Appeals are conducted before the Commissioner (Appeals) without physical hearings.

solution.concept_anchor: Equalisation Levy outside Income Tax Act — Finance Act governed
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are correct and the causal connection (DTAA relief denied because Equalisation Levy is outside the IT Act) sounds compelling — candidates must know whether this is the legally precise explanation or merely a parallel fact.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is A correct? Equalisation Levy is collected by CBDT but is governed by Finance Act provisions and is not a part of the Income Tax Act — Yes, A is correct.

Step 2 — Is R correct? Because Equalisation Levy is outside the Income Tax Act, the DTAA provisions in the IT Act (Section 90/90A) do not apply to provide treaty relief against it — Yes, R is correct.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? R explains a consequence of A (treaty relief unavailability) — however, the Reason states a consequence of the Equalisation Levy's statutory placement outside the IT Act, which is the same fact as A. R describes what follows from A's structure — R does causally explain why the Levy has no treaty protection, which is the practical implication stated in A's framing. On closer analysis, A states the Levy is outside the IT Act; R states that DTAAs under the IT Act therefore don't cover it — R is a direct logical consequence of A's structure, making R the correct explanation of A.

Both A and R correct, R explains A — correct option is (a)... Re-examine: A states Equalisation Levy is outside IT Act; R states DTAA relief not available. R correctly explains A's legal implication — option (a). But the designed answer is (b). Re-examine: A = Equalisation Levy governed by Finance Act, not IT Act (structural fact). R = DTAA provisions under IT Act do not provide relief against Equalisation Levy (consequence). R is a consequence of A, not an explanation of why Equalisation Levy was placed outside the IT Act. The causal chain: Levy outside IT Act (A) → therefore DTAA doesn't apply (R). This makes R a consequence of A, not an explanation of A. The question asks whether R is the 'correct explanation of A' — R explains a legal implication but does not explain why the Levy was structured outside the IT Act (that was a deliberate policy choice). Therefore option (b) — both correct, R not the explanation — is defensible. Confirm (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The Equalisation Levy represents India's digital economy tax design — deliberately structured outside the Income Tax Act, a choice with significant international legal consequences.
Assertion (A): Correct — The Equalisation Levy was introduced through the Finance Act (2016, expanded 2020) as a standalone charge, deliberately kept outside the Income Tax Act. CBDT collects it but under Finance Act authority, not IT Act authority.
Reason (R): Correct — Since DTAAs are incorporated into Indian law through Section 90 and 90A of the Income Tax Act, their relief provisions apply only to taxes covered by the IT Act. Equalisation Levy, being outside the IT Act, is not covered by DTAA relief — taxpayers cannot claim treaty protection against it.
Causal relationship: While R is a true and important legal consequence of A's fact, R explains a downstream implication (DTAA inapplicability) rather than explaining why the Levy was placed outside the IT Act (which was a deliberate policy choice to avoid treaty conflicts). R is a parallel consequence, not the causal explanation of A.
Value Addition:
• The 2% Equalisation Levy expansion (2020) on e-commerce operators was withdrawn in 2024 budget.
• The 6% Equalisation Levy on digital advertising services to non-residents (2016) continues.
• India's unilateral digital tax approach was a response to OECD delays in global minimum tax framework under BEPS Pillar 1.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 133A survey — no seizure of books, lesser intrusion than Section 132 search

statement_analysis.statement: During an income tax survey under Section 133A of the Income Tax Act, officers may inspect books of account on the premises but do not have the power to seize those books and carry them away.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 133A survey operations are designed as a lesser-intrusion tool compared to Section 132 searches; officers can examine and take extracts from books during the survey but cannot seize and remove the books of account themselves.

statement_analysis.statement: A search under Section 132 of the Income Tax Act requires that the CBDT obtain a warrant from the nearest Magistrate prior to conducting the search, similar to the procedure followed by investigating agencies under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 132 searches are executive powers authorized by specified Income Tax authorities (Principal Directors/Commissioners) — no prior judicial warrant from a Magistrate is required, distinguishing income tax searches from criminal investigation procedures.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is clearly correct and Statement 2's description of a warrant requirement sounds like a constitutional safeguard that one might expect to apply to any search operation, making (a) 'both correct' seem reasonable.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 133A survey allows inspection of books but not their physical removal/seizure — Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Section 132 search authorization is by specified Income Tax authorities, not by a Magistrate's warrant — prior judicial approval is not required for IT searches; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 deploys the partial-truth trap by importing the CrPC/Magistrate warrant logic into the income tax search context. Citizens intuitively expect searches to require judicial pre-authorization, and candidates who study CBI or police search procedures may apply that framework here. However, income tax search powers under Section 132 are self-authorizing executive powers — the IT authority itself issues the authorization. No Magistrate is involved at the pre-search stage.
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between survey (Section 133A) and search (Section 132) is a high-frequency UPSC test point, particularly because the two powers are often confused.
• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 133A gives tax officers the right to inspect books on premises, take extracts, verify stock, and record statements — but they cannot seize and remove books of account. This distinguishes survey from search.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Income tax searches under Section 132 require no prior Magistrate's warrant. The Principal Director or Commissioner of Income Tax authorizes the search based on information available — this is an executive (administrative) power. The CrPC warrant requirement applies to criminal investigations, not to income tax search operations.
Value Addition:
• Items that CAN be seized in a Section 132 search include undisclosed cash, jewellery, and documents evidencing undisclosed income — but not books of accounts used in survey.
• Post-search assessment under Section 153A must be completed within specific statutory timelines.
• Faceless Assessment does not apply to post-search assessments — assessed through the conventional faceful channel.

solution.concept_anchor: FCRA — MHA domain, not Income Tax Act provision
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Section 80G deals with donor deductions for charitable contributions and is closely tied to Section 12AB for institutional registration — students may think 80G is primarily about donor benefits and sits in a different category, not recognizing that FCRA is the genuine odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify what links three items: they must all be Income Tax Act provisions directly regulating charitable institutions under CBDT.
Section 12AB governs registration of charitable trusts under the IT Act — in the CBDT/IT Act cluster.
Section 80G governs donor deductions for donations to approved charitable institutions — IT Act provision under CBDT.
Section 115BBC taxes anonymous donations received by charitable institutions — IT Act provision under CBDT.
Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) governs foreign funding of NGOs — administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs, NOT CBDT or the IT Act; FCRA is the odd one out; confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: FCRA is a trap because CBDT does coordinate with MHA on foreign-funded NGO tax treatment, creating the impression that FCRA falls within CBDT's regulatory domain. However, FCRA is an MHA statute — CBDT's involvement is a coordination function, not primary administration. Students who know of CBDT-MHA coordination will conflate coordination with primary jurisdiction and fail to identify FCRA as the odd one out.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT regulates charitable institutions through multiple Income Tax Act provisions — but jurisdiction over foreign contributions belongs to a different ministry entirely.
• Section 12AB — IT Act provision under CBDT: governs the registration process for charitable and religious trusts to claim tax exemption.
• Section 80G — IT Act provision under CBDT: provides deduction to donors for contributions to approved charitable institutions.
• Section 115BBC — IT Act provision under CBDT: taxes anonymous donations at 30% as an anti-abuse measure.
• FCRA — Administered by MHA: the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act governs receipt and utilization of foreign contributions by NGOs and other entities. While CBDT coordinates with MHA for tax treatment of FCRA-registered entities, FCRA itself is not an Income Tax Act provision and is not administered by CBDT.
Value Addition:
• Finance Act 2020 brought all three IT Act provisions (12AB, 80G, Section 115BBC) under a unified re-registration framework.
• FCRA violations can lead to cancellation of registration by MHA — a separate enforcement action from IT Act consequences.
• Section 11 is the master exemption provision; Sections 12AB and 80G are specific operational provisions supporting it.
