solution.concept_anchor: Section 194P — senior citizen TDS exemption from ITR filing
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because senior citizens do receive special treatment under income tax law, and the instinct that 'senior citizens are exempt from all compliance requirements' sounds plausible given the policy direction of reducing compliance burden.
elimination_logic: Identify the scenario: a 76-year-old with only pension and interest income whose bank deducts TDS — this precisely matches the Section 194P scenario.
Eliminate (a): Senior citizens above 75 are not exempted from all income tax liability — they remain taxable; the exemption is from ITR filing, not from tax itself.
Eliminate (b): There is no provision requiring automatic CBDT assessment for senior citizens not filing returns.
Eliminate (d): Section 80TTB provides a higher deduction on interest income for senior citizens but does not address ITR filing exemption.
Section 194P: Specified senior citizens (75+) with only pension and interest income from the same bank are exempted from filing ITR if the bank deducts appropriate TDS — confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) exploits scope-extension: 'all income tax compliance requirements' is too broad. Section 194P exempts qualifying senior citizens only from the ITR filing obligation — they still pay tax (through TDS). Candidates who know 'senior citizens get relaxation in 2021' but don't know the precise scope of that relaxation will over-generalise and select (a), missing that the provision is ITR-filing specific, not a blanket tax exemption.
solution.final_explanation:
Section 194P, introduced by the Finance Act 2021, was a targeted CBDT-administered relief for a specific category of senior citizens.
The scenario describes a 75+ year-old with only pension and FD interest from one bank — precisely the qualifying profile for Section 194P.
• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 194P does not exempt senior citizens from all income tax compliance or from tax liability — it exempts only from the ITR filing obligation if the bank deducts appropriate TDS covering all their income.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: No provision requires CBDT to conduct automatic assessments for senior citizens who do not file; Section 194P eliminates the filing obligation itself where conditions are met.
• Option (c) — Correct: Section 194P requires the specified bank (paying pension and interest) to compute total income, deduct appropriate TDS, and file a declaration — the senior citizen is then relieved of ITR filing.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Section 80TTB provides a higher interest income deduction (up to Rs 50,000) for senior citizens but is a deduction provision, not an ITR-filing exemption mechanism.
Value Addition:
• Qualifying conditions: age 75+, only pension from one bank, interest from the same bank, resident individual.
• The bank files a declaration with CBDT on behalf of such senior citizens.
• Section 80TTB (interest deduction for seniors) and Section 194P (ITR filing exemption) are complementary but separate provisions.

solution.concept_anchor: DTAA beneficial rule and GAAR override of treaty benefits

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 90(2) of the Income Tax Act, a taxpayer has the option to be governed by whichever is more beneficial — the provisions of the applicable DTAA or the provisions of domestic income tax law.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 90(2) enshrines the 'most beneficial' principle — the taxpayer may apply whichever set of provisions (treaty or domestic) results in lower tax liability, making DTAA application optional and taxpayer-driven.

statement_analysis.statement: India's General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR) cannot override the benefits available to a taxpayer under a Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement, since DTAA provisions have been held to be superior to domestic anti-avoidance measures.
statement_analysis.reason: GAAR can override DTAA benefits in cases where the arrangement is identified as an impermissible avoidance arrangement — GAAR is specifically designed to deny treaty benefits claimed through artificial structures, making the absolute claim of treaty supremacy over GAAR incorrect.

statement_analysis.statement: Transfer pricing regulations under Sections 92 to 92F of the Income Tax Act empower CBDT to prescribe methods for computing the arm's length price in cross-border transactions between associated enterprises.
statement_analysis.reason: Sections 92–92F constitute India's transfer pricing framework, under which CBDT prescribes the recognised methods (CUP, cost-plus, TNMM, etc.) for determining arm's length prices and the documentation requirements for taxpayers.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because the statement that 'DTAAs are superior to domestic law' sounds like a correct extension of Section 90(2)'s beneficial rule — students who know Section 90(2) grants DTAA supremacy when beneficial may overgeneralise to conclude GAAR cannot override DTAAs.
elimination_logic: Read the question: it asks which statement(s) are NOT correct.
Statement 1: Section 90(2)'s most-beneficial principle is accurately stated — Statement 1 is correct (not the answer).
Statement 2: GAAR CAN override DTAA benefits when arrangements are impermissible avoidance structures — the absolute claim that GAAR 'cannot override' DTAA is incorrect; Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: CBDT's power to prescribe arm's length methods under Sections 92–92F is accurately described — Statement 3 is correct (not the answer).
Only Statement 2 is NOT correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the overgeneralisation of Section 90(2)'s beneficial rule. The rule says DTAA applies when more beneficial — but GAAR is a separate instrument that can deny benefits from transactions that are impermissible avoidance arrangements. The Indian government specifically clarified that GAAR overrides treaty benefits in cases of treaty shopping and artificial avoidance structures. The 'always superior' characterization of DTAA against GAAR is the precise scope-extension error UPSC exploits.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's international taxation toolkit involves both facilitative instruments (DTAAs, APAs) and anti-avoidance tools (GAAR, transfer pricing), and their interaction is a nuanced exam area.
• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 90(2) grants taxpayers the choice between treaty provisions and domestic law — whichever is more beneficial applies. This is the foundational DTAA principle.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: GAAR is not subordinate to DTAA provisions when an arrangement constitutes an impermissible avoidance arrangement. India clarified through the Finance Act 2013 amendments that GAAR can deny treaty benefits claimed through artificial structures — GAAR was specifically designed to address treaty shopping.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Transfer pricing under Sections 92–92F gives CBDT authority to prescribe arm's length price computation methods, documentation norms, and safe harbour rules.
Value Addition:
• Countries with which India has DTAAs exceeding 90 — among the largest treaty networks globally.
• Safe Harbour Rules under transfer pricing allow CBDT to prescribe predetermined margins for specific industries/transactions.
• The distinction between GAAR (general) and SAAR (Specific Anti-Avoidance Rules like thin-capitalisation, CFC rules) is a growing UPSC focus.

solution.concept_anchor: Major CBDT-administered tax reforms — chronological sequence
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who remember 'corporate tax cut was recent and GST came before it' may place the GST transition ahead of Wealth Tax abolition without checking the precise 2015 date of Wealth Tax abolition relative to CBEC→CBIC renaming.
elimination_logic: Wealth Tax was abolished in the Union Budget 2015 (Finance Act 2015) — this is the earliest event among these four.
CBEC was renamed CBIC in 2018 following the GST rollout in July 2017 — second in sequence.
Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance 2019 cut corporate tax to 22%/15% — third event.
Section 115BAC (New Tax Regime for individuals) was introduced in Finance Act 2020 — fourth and latest event.
Correct sequence: Wealth Tax abolition (2015) → CBEC renamed CBIC (2018) → Corporate tax cut ordinance (2019) → Section 115BAC (2020) = option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The CBEC→CBIC renaming in 2018 is a commonly mis-placed event — candidates who anchor on 'GST = 2017' place the renaming in 2017 rather than 2018, shifting the entire sequence. Similarly, Wealth Tax abolition in 2015 is sometimes conflated with demonetization (2016) or GST-era changes. Each event in this chronology has a precise year that UPSC tests through sequence questions.
solution.final_explanation:
These four events span the key tax reform milestones from 2015 to 2020, all involving CBDT and CBIC's administrative domains.
Correct sequence:
1. Wealth Tax abolished (2015): The Finance Act 2015 abolished the Wealth Tax Act, eliminating a tax that CBDT administered.
2. CBEC renamed CBIC (2018): Following the GST rollout in July 2017, the Central Board of Excise and Customs was renamed the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs in 2018 to reflect its expanded mandate.
3. Corporate tax rate cut — Taxation Laws (Amendment) Ordinance (September 2019): Reduced the corporate tax rate to 22% for existing companies (Section 115BAA) and 15% for new manufacturing companies (Section 115BAB).
4. Section 115BAC introduced (Finance Act 2020): The new optional tax regime for individuals with lower rates but no exemptions — the most recent among these four.
Why wrong options fail:
• (b) and (d) place CBIC renaming before Wealth Tax abolition — incorrect.
• (c) places the corporate tax cut before CBIC renaming — incorrect sequence.
Value Addition:
• Wealth Tax abolition was accompanied by enhanced reporting requirements for high-value assets in ITR forms.
• Section 115BAC was made the default regime for individuals from AY 2024-25.
• India's corporate tax rate of 22% (effective ~25.17% with surcharge) is now comparable to global averages.

solution.concept_anchor: Binoy Viswam case — Aadhaar-PAN linkage upheld, Section 139AA
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because the Puttaswamy case (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India) is the landmark Aadhaar judgment and candidates conflate it with the PAN-specific judgment, not knowing that PAN-Aadhaar linkage was specifically challenged and upheld in the separate Binoy Viswam case.
elimination_logic: Identify which Supreme Court case specifically dealt with the constitutional validity of mandatory Aadhaar-PAN linking under Section 139AA.
Eliminate (a): The Maneka Gandhi case relates to Article 21 and personal liberty — not Aadhaar-PAN.
Eliminate (b): K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India was the broader Aadhaar constitutionality challenge and privacy right case — not specifically the PAN-Aadhaar section.
Eliminate (d): UCO Bank case established that CBDT Circulars cannot override statute — unrelated to Aadhaar-PAN.
Binoy Viswam v. Union of India (2017) specifically upheld Section 139AA's mandatory Aadhaar-PAN linking — confirm (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Puttaswamy case is the most famous Aadhaar-related Supreme Court judgment and draws nearly all student attention when Aadhaar constitutionality is mentioned. However, the Puttaswamy case (9-judge bench, 2017) addressed the right to privacy and broader Aadhaar constitutionality, while the specific question of Aadhaar-PAN mandatory linkage under Section 139AA was adjudicated in the earlier (also 2017) Binoy Viswam v. Union of India case. UPSC rewards this entity-level precision.
solution.final_explanation:
Mandatory Aadhaar-PAN linkage under Section 139AA was a significant policy measure that faced immediate legal challenge, resolved by a specific Supreme Court judgment.
• Option (a) — Incorrect: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) concerns Article 21 and the right to travel abroad — not related to Aadhaar or PAN.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India addressed the broader Aadhaar Act's constitutionality and established privacy as a fundamental right — it is not the specific case on Section 139AA PAN-Aadhaar linking.
• Option (c) — Correct: Binoy Viswam v. Union of India (2017) is the Supreme Court case that specifically challenged and upheld the constitutional validity of Section 139AA's mandatory Aadhaar-PAN linkage.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: UCO Bank case deals with the binding force of CBDT Circulars — entirely unrelated to Aadhaar or PAN.
Value Addition:
• PAN inoperativity (post non-linking) results in higher TDS rates and inability to open bank accounts for taxable transactions.
• CBDT extended the PAN-Aadhaar linking deadline multiple times before the June 2023 final deadline.
• Aadhaar-PAN linkage enables de-duplication of PANs — a significant tax administration benefit.

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT enforcement statutes — Black Money Act, Benami Act, IT Act provisions

statement_analysis.statement: The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015 is administered by CBDT and targets specifically offshore undisclosed income and assets — not domestic undisclosed income.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2015 Act has a specific and exclusive focus on foreign (offshore) undisclosed assets and income; domestic undisclosed income is dealt with under the Income Tax Act and through schemes like IDS 2016, not the 2015 Black Money Act.

statement_analysis.statement: The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 converted benami transaction adjudication into a quasi-judicial function performed by an Adjudicating Authority, separate from CBDT's administrative role.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2016 Amendment Act created an Adjudicating Authority as a quasi-judicial body for benami cases — CBDT's income tax investigation units may initiate proceedings but adjudication is by an independent body, separating enforcement from adjudication.

statement_analysis.statement: The Income Declaration Scheme, 2016 provided immunity from prosecution under all laws, including the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), to those who disclosed undisclosed domestic income.
statement_analysis.reason: IDS 2016 provided immunity from Income Tax Act prosecution and specific penalty provisions, but it did NOT provide blanket immunity from FEMA, PMLA, or other special laws — declarations under IDS 2016 remained subject to these other statutes.

statement_analysis.statement: Section 115BBC of the Income Tax Act applies a flat tax rate of 30% on anonymous donations received by charitable institutions, serving as an anti-abuse provision to prevent money laundering through the charitable sector.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 115BBC taxes anonymous donations at 30% — correctly stated; the provision prevents misuse of the charitable trust route for introduction of unaccounted funds.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is the strong distractor because Statement 3 contains an accurate core (IDS 2016 gave immunity) and the scope-extension to PMLA/FEMA may not be immediately identifiable as wrong by candidates who don't know the exact scope of IDS immunity.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Black Money Act 2015 targets foreign assets only, not domestic — correct.
Statement 2: Benami adjudication is by an Adjudicating Authority, separate from CBDT — correct.
Statement 3: IDS 2016 immunity did NOT extend to PMLA and FEMA — the 'all laws' claim is a scope-extension error; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4: Section 115BBC taxing anonymous donations at 30% is accurately stated — correct.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4) — answer is Only three = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a partial-truth trap: IDS 2016 did provide immunity from Income Tax prosecution — which many candidates know. The false extension is that this immunity covered 'all laws including FEMA and PMLA.' Voluntary disclosure schemes in India have consistently carved out PMLA and FEMA from immunity, precisely to prevent the schemes from becoming money-laundering shields. Candidates who know IDS gave immunity but don't know its precise scope will accept the broad statement as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
CBDT's enforcement portfolio spans multiple special statutes with distinct scopes and procedural characters.
• Statement 1 — Correct: The 2015 Black Money Act is exclusively for foreign undisclosed assets — domestic black money remains under the IT Act.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The 2016 Benami Act Amendment created independent Adjudicating Authorities — CBDT investigates but does not adjudicate benami cases.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: IDS 2016 immunity was limited to Income Tax Act penalties and prosecution — it explicitly did NOT provide immunity under FEMA, PMLA, or other special statutes. Declarants remained exposed to those laws.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Section 115BBC's 30% flat tax on anonymous donations is accurately described.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct.
Value Addition:
• Under the Black Money Act 2015, the combined tax and penalty can reach 90% of undisclosed foreign assets.
• Benami property upon confiscation vests in the Central Government — not in CBDT.
• IDS 2016 attracted approximately ₹65,000 crore in disclosures — a significant revenue collection.

solution.concept_anchor: Faceless Assessment — Section 144B of Income Tax Act
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Section 143(3) is the provision most associated with regular income tax scrutiny assessments, and candidates who know Faceless Assessment operates within the scrutiny assessment framework may name Section 143(3) as the provision rather than Section 144B which was the specific section inserted for the faceless scheme.
elimination_logic: The blank refers to the specific Income Tax Act section under which the Faceless Assessment Scheme operates — a specific section was inserted for this purpose.
Eliminate (a): Section 132 governs search and seizure — unrelated to faceless assessments.
Eliminate (b): Section 143(3) governs regular scrutiny assessments — Faceless Assessment is conducted under a specific separate provision.
Eliminate (c): Section 115BAC governs the new individual tax regime — unrelated to assessment procedure.
Section 144B was specifically inserted into the Income Tax Act as the enabling provision for Faceless Assessment — confirm (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Section 143(3) is the exam-well-known scrutiny assessment provision, and Faceless Assessment is indeed a form of scrutiny — making (b) feel intuitively correct. Section 144B is a less-commonly-cited provision that was specifically inserted to create the faceless assessment framework. UPSC rewards candidates who know the specific enabling section rather than the general category of assessment it belongs to.
solution.final_explanation:
The Faceless Assessment Scheme required specific statutory authority, achieved through an amendment inserting a new provision into the Income Tax Act.
• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 132 authorises search and seizure operations — a completely different enforcement tool with no connection to faceless assessment.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Section 143(3) governs regular (non-faceless) scrutiny assessments; while Faceless Assessment is a form of scrutiny, it operates under a distinct provision inserted specifically for this purpose.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Section 115BAC introduced the new optional individual tax regime — a substantive tax provision, not a procedural assessment provision.
• Option (d) — Correct: Section 144B was specifically inserted into the Income Tax Act to provide the legal architecture for the Faceless Assessment Scheme, including the random allocation of cases, team-based assessment, and the review mechanism.
Value Addition:
• Faceless Assessment eliminates geographical jurisdiction — a taxpayer in Chennai may be assessed by an officer in Delhi.
• The review unit under Section 144B can flag assessment orders before they are issued.
• Section 144B explicitly lists categories excluded from Faceless Assessment including search cases and international tax matters.

solution.concept_anchor: CBDT advisory vs decision-making — Finance Minister decides, CBDT recommends

statement_analysis.statement: CBDT's role in the Union Budget process is primarily advisory — it provides direct tax revenue projections and recommendations on exemption rationalization to the Finance Ministry, but the final decisions on tax rates and exemptions rest with the Finance Minister.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT is an administrative body under the Finance Ministry; it prepares inputs including revenue estimates and policy options but the ultimate fiscal decisions, reflected in the Finance Bill, are made by the Finance Minister and Cabinet.

statement_analysis.statement: Because CBDT exercises administrative control over the Income Tax Department and its field formations, CBDT also has the authority to decide on tax exemptions and deduction limits that appear in the annual Finance Act, subject only to parliamentary ratification.
statement_analysis.reason: CBDT has no authority to decide tax exemptions or deduction limits — these are legislative and fiscal policy decisions made by the Finance Ministry and enacted through the Finance Bill; CBDT's role is purely advisory and operational, not decision-making on legislative tax provisions.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because CBDT's immense operational authority over the Income Tax Department makes it feel like a co-decision-maker in tax policy, not merely an advisor — candidates who know CBDT has significant power conflate operational authority with fiscal policy decision-making authority.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: CBDT provides projections and recommendations — Finance Minister decides; this correctly describes the advisory-decision split; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: CBDT 'deciding on tax exemptions' subject to parliamentary ratification overstates CBDT's role — the Finance Ministry decides, not CBDT; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a scope-extension trap: CBDT does recommend exemption rationalization, and CBDT does prepare extensive tax expenditure analysis. The false leap is that 'recommending' becomes 'deciding' — with 'subject to parliamentary ratification' adding false legitimacy. CBDT is strictly advisory in the fiscal policy space; no provision exists for CBDT to independently decide what appears in the Finance Act. This is a governance precision point UPSC tests to distinguish administrative authority from fiscal policy authority.
solution.final_explanation:
The advisory-decision boundary between CBDT and the Finance Ministry is a subtle but important governance distinction.
• Statement 1 — Correct: CBDT's budget-related role is input provision — revenue projections, tax expenditure analysis, and recommendations on exemptions. The Finance Minister, supported by the Ministry of Finance's budget division, makes the actual decisions codified in the Finance Bill.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: CBDT has no authority to decide on tax exemptions, deduction limits, or rate changes — these are legislative and fiscal policy decisions. The 'subject to parliamentary ratification' qualifier does not create an intermediate CBDT decision-making role; it is the Finance Ministry, not CBDT, that proposes what Parliament ratifies.
Value Addition:
• The Revenue Secretary (not CBDT Chairman) leads the Finance Ministry's revenue policy coordination.
• Tax Expenditure Statement prepared by CBDT quantifies revenue foregone — it influences but does not determine the Finance Minister's decisions.
• The distinction between administrative autonomy and fiscal policy authority applies similarly to SEBI (regulatory) vs. Finance Ministry (policy) in the securities market context.
